paras: Renata Vidal is a lawyer from Belo Horizonte, and this year she is doing something she planned for a long time. She is currently living in Amsterdam, where she is in her first semester of a master's degree in international trade law, and she is still working two mornings a week for her firm in Brazil. She says the hardest part is not the English. It is the calendar.

Her week rarely looks the same twice. On Monday and Wednesday she attends seminars in the morning. On Tuesday she is usually in the library, because she is researching delivery clauses for her thesis, and she is two weeks behind. Her supervisor is reading the first proposal this week, and Renata is waiting for his comments before she submits anything else. She says the progress is real, but nobody sees it from outside.

The firm in Brazil is not waiting for her. Two colleagues are handling her cases while she is away, and they send her an update every Friday. This month they are preparing a contract for a client who imports fertilizer, and Renata is reviewing the difficult clauses at night, from Amsterdam. She does not charge for those hours. She is not doing it for the money; she is doing it so that the clients are still hers when she goes back.

Two of her friends in Brazil are applying to the same program for next year, and they ask her the same question every week: is it worth it? She never answers immediately. She is tired, the workload is heavier than she expected, and she is spending more than she planned. But she is also reading contracts that nobody sends her in Brazil, and she is reading them in the language they were written in. That, she says, is the whole point.
reading.source: A composite portrait of a Brazilian lawyer in her first year abroad, written for this lesson.

choices: To explain how to get a master's degree in the Netherlands.
To show what one semester abroad actually looks like week by week, for somebody who is still working.
To argue that Brazilian lawyers should study abroad.

items.situation: Say what Renata does every week, and then what she is doing this week. Two sentences.
tips: She attends seminars on Monday and Wednesday. This week she is waiting for her supervisor's comments.
The first is a habit, the second is now. Two different tenses, on purpose.

items.situation: Somebody asks: are you working on anything right now?
tips: I am currently working on an import contract for a client in Santos.
Not: I currently work. If it is this month only, it needs am/is/are plus -ing.

items.situation: Say one thing that is temporary in your office at the moment.
tips: My associate is handling two of my cases this month, because I am preparing an application.
Temporary is exactly what this tense is for.

items.situation: Correct me. I say: 'I am usually reviewing contracts on Monday mornings.'
tips: I usually review contracts on Monday mornings.
Usually means habit, and a habit takes present simple. The two do not go together.

items.situation: Ask me two questions about what I am doing this month.
tips: What are you working on at the moment?
Are you applying to any program this year?

items.situation: Say what is happening in your market right now, in one sentence.
tips: Prices are going up, and a lot of ships are waiting outside the port.
This is the sentence a seminar asks you for every single week.

listenings.text: Hello, this is a message for the students of the international trade group. I am recording it on Sunday evening, because a few things are changing this week. First, Professor Lindqvist is traveling, so Tuesday's seminar is moving to Thursday, at the same time. Second, we are still waiting for four thesis proposals. If you are working on yours right now, do not worry about the length. Send me the two pages you have and we will talk. Third, the library is closing early all week, because they are installing new equipment on the second floor. And one last thing. Two of you are asking me the same question about the reading list, so I am putting the answer in writing tomorrow morning. Please read that email before you write to me again. Thank you.

Right now, while we are talking, about two hundred ships are waiting outside Brazilian ports, and most of them are carrying corn or soybeans. That number is going up every week at this time of year, and it tells you more about the market than any price on a screen does. Here is why. A trader is not only buying a product. He is buying a date. If a ship is sitting outside Santos for eleven days instead of three, somebody is paying for those eight days, and the contract decides who. So when people ask me what is happening in the grain market this month, I never start with the price. I start with the queue. The queue is the market talking, and at the moment it is saying that everybody is in a hurry.
